text:
With the signing of the Paris Agreement in 2015, which took effect in November 20161, the global focus has shifted towards reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to combat climate change. For policymakers, mitigating emissions has become essential for not only meeting environmental goals but also addressing the economic implications of climate policies2. Emission reduction strategies in sectors like transportation are increasingly evaluated through GHG abatement curves, which help identify the most cost-effective approaches to emissions control3. These tools are vital in formulating policies that balance environmental objectives with economic viability.

Studies indicate that the road transport sector emitted 5.0 GtCO2e (Gigatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalent, the unit used to measure greenhouse gas emissions on a large scale) annually in 2005, increasing to 8.7 GtCO2e by 2019, representing 23% of global energy-related CO2 emissions4. Road vehicles contribute around 70% of these emissions, underscoring the need for policy interventions that target emissions reductions in this sector5. To meet regulatory standards, vehicle manufacturers have responded with technological advancements, including improved internal combustion engines and the development of hybrid and electric vehicles6. Beyond technological solutions, policymakers can benefit from planning and operational strategies to reduce emissions and cost in transportation systems. For example, energy efficiency analysis in regional transport sectors provides insights into emissions reduction opportunities7. Behavioral interventions, including fiscal incentives and public information campaigns, also encourage travelers to choose less polluting modes8. Additionally, operational strategies like zero-emission delivery vehicles and shared mobility services provide targeted solutions for reducing urban congestion and emissions9,10,11. Optimizing traffic flow through behavioral and system management strategies, such as traffic assignment and speed control, can significantly reduce emissions without requiring additional infrastructure investment12. Traffic assignment (TA) aims to determine the distribution of traffic flow over the transportation network. Consequently, the economic and environmental benefits of enhancing road transportation efficiency are evident, reinforcing the value of policy-driven traffic management strategies. In this paper, we focus on speed control and traffic assignment to achieve substantial emission reductions through improved traffic flow and route optimization to reveal the potential of policy applications for reducing emissions.

A road transportation network comprises interconnected routes facilitating vehicle movement between various locations. Travelers select routes based on factors such as travel time and distance, aiming to minimize their travel time or associated costs13. Traffic assignment problem (TAP) models provide a systematic framework for allocating travel demand across these origin-destination (OD) pairs, estimating traffic flow on each road segment. One of the foundational studies in this domain is14 which analyzed traffic flows in urban transportation networks using a Beckmann-based approach and Frank-Wolfe’s convex combinations method to solve the User Equilibrium (UE) problem, where no traveler can reduce their travel time by switching routes. This foundational approach assumes single-class, single-mode traffic; however, in real-world applications, multiple transportation modes share routes, necessitating a multi-modal, multi-class approach to capture realistic dynamics15. extended this model to accommodate various transportation modes, focusing on travel time optimization across multiple classes using a multi-class (MC) UE problem as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem. Their approach demonstrated significant improvements over the traditional Beckmann-based framework. Similarly16, developed a Dynamic Traffic Assignment (DTA) model to better capture the features of multi-class traffic flow, highlighting the complexities of realistic network behavior that remain under-explored in the current research landscape.

While a number of studies have analyzed multi-class traffic assignment models, there is currently no work, to our knowledge, that incorporates multi-class speed control (SC) within an integrated optimization framework. Our study addresses this gap by developing a novel multi-modal, multi-class speed control model that jointly optimizes both path flows and free-flow speeds to minimize emissions and travel time. This is particularly impactful in the context of networks with longer links, where speed control can be more effectively implemented and enforced. Even in networks with shorter links, this approach could become feasible and practical through increased vehicle automation and connected vehicle technologies, which enable rapid, adaptive speed control. This methodology represents a new avenue for low-emission traffic planning, particularly in scenarios where physical infrastructure changes are limited or costly.

This work adopts a Static Traffic Assignment (STA) setting. Link travel times and speeds represent steady-state (e.g., peak-period average) conditions for a given OD matrix and speed-limit policy. TAP models are thus critical for optimizing traffic flow, alleviating congestion, and minimizing travel time, with direct implications for the economic efficiency of transportation systems. When coupled with emission models, TAP models further provide insights into the environmental impacts of traffic, allowing planners to balance flow efficiency with emissions reduction. The existing literature offers a range of approaches: some adopt a single-objective focus on travel time or congestion reduction to estimate exhaust emissions17,18, while others use a bi-objective approach, optimizing both emission reduction and traffic flow efficiency19,20,21,22,23,24,25.

These studies contribute to the understanding of efficient traffic flow and environmental impact, suggesting strategies that support emission abatement and economically viable traffic management. The current focus has shifted toward employing advanced traffic management systems to explore the economic implications of emission abatement, allowing policymakers to design strategies, such as speed limits, that incentivize eco-friendly driving behaviors. Traffic distribution under UE conditions serves as a reference point for these strategies.

While optimizing the system based on collective goals refers to the classical system optimum (SO), where total travel time is minimized without imposing any behavioural constraints, this ideal benchmark is rarely attainable in practice because users behave selfishly and follow UE-type route choices. In this study, we therefore do not enforce a free, unconstrained SO; instead, we minimise system-level objectives (travel time and emissions) within the set of flows that satisfy UE or BRUE conditions. In other words, our traffic management strategies aim to move the system from a reference UE or BRUE state toward a behaviourally constrained system optimum, improving service quality and emissions while remaining consistent with user behaviour.

This study aims to bridge these gaps by proposing a unified modeling and optimization framework for multi-class speed control and traffic assignment, and by using this framework to compute carbon abatement curves. We provide traffic authorities with a policy tool that incorporates both environmental and behavioral realism, enabling them to design effective and cost-efficient management strategies based on system-level and bounded-rationality behavior.

In modeling how travelers choose their routes, we rely on the concept of UE, where no individual traveler can improve their travel time by unilaterally changing routes, commonly referred to as Wardrop’s first principle. The proposed approach applies system-optimal objectives over the path flow solution space consistent with user equilibrium link flows, enabling effective emission and travel time reductions while preserving user satisfaction.

Throughout the remainder of the paper, whenever we refer to scenario labels such as UE-SOTT+E, BRUE-SOTT, BRUE-SOTT+E, SC-UE-SOTT+E, or SC-BRUE-SOTT+E, the term SO should be understood as a system-level objective minimized subject to UE or BRUE constraints, rather than a classical unconstrained system optimum.

While UE assumes that all users have perfect information and make rational decisions, real-world behavior often deviates from this assumption26. To account for more realistic traveler behavior, we also incorporate Bounded Rationality User Equilibrium (BRUE), which allows users to tolerate a small difference in travel cost or time (called an indifference band), reflecting imperfect information, cognitive limitations, or personal preferences. This distinction enables more accurate modeling of route choice behavior under real-world conditions. The main contributions of this study are as follows:

We introduce a novel optimization framework for multi-class traffic assignment with joint speed control, addressing a critical gap in current transportation modeling literature.

We develop a comprehensive traffic management strategy to reduce carbon emissions within a multi-modal freeway network. This involves optimizing the flow of various transportation modes to achieve significant emission reductions.

We identify and analyze the balancing points between environmental goals and economic objectives. This ensures that our proposed strategies are both environmentally beneficial and economically viable.

We formulate and solve the network equilibrium problem for user optimum scenarios. Additionally, we optimize a combined travel-time and emission-cost objective by adjusting speed limits, demonstrating how regulatory measures can support lower-emission traffic management.

We consider Bounded Rationality User Equilibrium (BRUE) to account for the biases in users’ route choices. This provides a more realistic representation of the driver decision-making process, leading to more accurate and applicable traffic management strategies.

Beyond methodological novelty, we examine generalizability and scalability. Many emission-aware assignment and control approaches are validated only on small networks, which limits confidence in operational relevance at the metropolitan scale. We therefore complement the Tilburg freeway experiment with a full-scale application on the Melbourne GMNS freeway network. This second case allows us to test whether the proposed multi-class UE/BRUE formulations with speed control remain computationally tractable and policy-informative on a large network, and whether targeted optimization, acting only on a subset of high-demand OD pairs while evaluating impacts system-wide, can still deliver measurable travel-time and emission benefits.

This paper is organized as follows: the next section reviews the literature on traffic emission models and environmentally focused traffic management strategies. Section Methodology presents the methodology, including problem statement, network description, and mathematical formulation for user equilibrium (UE) and bounded rationality user equilibrium (BRUE). Section Emission model details the emission model and its linearization. Section Numerical Experiments provides and discusses the application of the proposed framework and the results. Finally, the conclusion section summarizes the findings and future research directions.

Overview

This section outlines the methods used to address the multi-class static traffic assignment problem, with a focus on emission reduction. We begin with a problem statement highlighting the need to differentiate between freight and passenger vehicles in emission studies. Then, we present a bi-objective optimization problem that targets both total travel time and emissions under Pure User Equilibrium (PRUE) and Bounded Rationality User Equilibrium (BRUE), formulated in a static setting where link flows and travel times represent steady-state (e.g., peak-period) conditions for a given OD demand. We then describe the traffic network properties using the Bureau of Public Roads (BPR) function to model relationships between traffic flow, road capacity, and congestion. In our framework, speed control is represented through free-flow speeds in the BPR functions, so that changes in speed limits impact the static travel times used by the assignment model. We detail the equilibria formulation, explaining the conditions for UE and BRUE.

Finally, we linearize the problem for implementation as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model. This approach enables us to assess the effects of various traffic management strategies on emissions and travel times.

Problem statement

The literature review shows that some models studying emissions assume all vehicles belong to the same class without considering engine differences, while others address a multi-class problem with simplified assignment or emission models. Since freight and passenger vehicles have distinct characteristics, it is crucial to assess how these differences impact emissions and determine which approach is best suited for our study.

Figure 1 demonstrates that the emission curves for cars and trucks differ significantly. Panel a compares emissions per vehicle kilometer as a function of speed, while panel b shows emissions on a 30 km road segment as a function of travel time. When comparing emissions by speed, freight vehicles emit more than passenger vehicles, with the gap widening to around 40 km/h. Similarly, pollution costs per vehicle vary with travel time, with truck emissions being up to 1.6 times higher than those of cars. This highlights the significant impact of traffic mode on emissions, underscoring the relevance of a multi-class traffic management model for both route choice and emission considerations.

In this context, we present the mathematical formulation for route-choice through a bi-objective optimization problem, focusing on minimizing total travel time (TTT) and emissions under PRUE and BRUE. Here, we outline the objective functions, constraints, and linearization of the problem, aiming to develop an equivalent Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation. Table 3 introduces the notations used in this paper.

Network formulation

The traffic network is represented by a graph consisting of a set of nodes, \({\mathcal{N}}\), and directed links, \({\mathcal{E}}\). Let \({\mathcal{W}}\) denote the Origin-Destination (OD) pair set. Between each OD pair \(w\in {\mathcal{W}}\), vehicles of classes \({\mathcal{M}}\) can travel via several paths \(p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}\), each composed of a sequence of distinct nodes. For a given class \(m\in {\mathcal{M}}\) and OD pair w, let \({f}_{p,w}^{m}\) denote the flow on path \(p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}\), \({x}_{e}^{m}\) the flow of link e for this OD pair, and \({d}_{w}^{m}\) the associated demand.

$$\begin{array}{cc}{x}_{e}^{m} > 0, & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},e\in {\mathcal{E}},\end{array}\,\,\,$$

(1)

$$\begin{array}{cc}{f}_{p,w}^{m}\ge 0, & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},w\in {\mathcal{W}},p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w},\end{array}\,\,$$

(2)

$$\begin{array}{cc}{x}_{e}^{m}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{w\in {\mathcal{W}}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}}{\delta }_{p,e}{f}_{p,w}^{m}, & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},e\in {\mathcal{E}},\end{array}\,\,\,$$

(3)

$$\begin{array}{cc}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}}{f}_{p,w}^{m}={d}_{w}^{m}, & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},w\in {\mathcal{W}},\end{array}\,\,\,$$

(4)

Where the adjacency matrix of coefficients is,

$${\delta }_{p,e}=\left\{\begin{array}{l}1,\,\mathrm{if}\mathrm{link}\,e\,\mathrm{belongs}\mathrm{to}\mathrm{path}\,p\,,\,\\ 0,\,\mathrm{otherwise}\,,\end{array}\right.\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w},\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(5)

The parameter πm represents the Passenger Car Equivalent (PCE), which is 1 for m = 1 (car) and 2.5 for m = 2 (truck). Let α = 0.15andβ = 4 be additional parameters for the BPR function. Denote Ke and Le the capacity and length of link e, respectively. The freeflow speed of class m on link e is \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\), and the associated freeflow travel time is \({T}_{e}^{m}=\frac{{L}_{e}}{{v}_{e,0}^{m}}\), representing the minimum possible travel time in the absence of congestion. The freeflow speed \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\) can be a decision variable determined by the speed limit.

The BPR function models the relationship between traffic flow, road capacity, and congestion. It allows the calculation of travel time and is defined as:

$$\begin{array}{cc}{c}_{e}^{m}={T}_{e}^{m}\left(1+\alpha {\left(\mathop{\sum }\limits_{m\in {\mathcal{M}}}\frac{{x}_{e}^{m}{\pi }^{m}}{{K}_{e}}\right)}^{\beta }\right), & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.\end{array}\,$$

(6)

In our setting, these travel times represent average steady-state conditions for a given demand matrix and set of speed limits; no time-dependent dynamics (e.g., propagation of congestion over time) are modeled.

Our primary focus is on minimization of travel time. In our study \({c}_{p,w}^{m}\) is the time cost for users belonging to class m travelling between OD pair w through path p, and \({c}_{w}^{m* }\) is the minimum time cost. Thus,

$$\begin{array}{cc}{c}_{p,w}^{m}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{e\in {\mathcal{E}}}{\delta }_{p,e}{c}_{e}^{m}, & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}},\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w},\end{array}\,$$

(7)

$$\begin{array}{cc}{c}_{w}^{m* }=\min \{\mathop{\mathop{c}\limits^{m}}\limits_{p,w}\,| \,p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}\}, & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}}.\end{array}\,$$

(8)

The chosen framework is TAP, meaning that the distribution of flow through links takes place in a system under equilibrium. Wardrop’s principles are fundamental concepts in transportation theory, and each is associated with a specific equilibrium condition. These principles are at the core of this study. The First Principle, aligned with PRUE, asserts that in a state of equilibrium, the travel times on all routes that are used are equal and these travel times are less than or equal to the travel times on any unused routes. This reflects the idea that travelers choose routes that minimize their travel time60. The Second Principle, linked to System Optimum (SO), suggests that the overall efficiency of the transportation system is maximized when the average or total travel time for all travelers is minimized. This affirms that all users collaborate in their route choices to guarantee the optimal utilization of the entire system. This is further elaborated and formulated in the following sections.

User equilibrium

Pure Rational User Equilibrium (PRUE), commonly abbreviated as UE, represents a state where each traveler has perfect knowledge of current and future traffic conditions. In this state, travelers choose routes to minimize their personal travel time, disregarding the collective impact on traffic congestion. This optimization problem was formulated by ref. 61.

For the previously defined traffic network, the user-equilibrium conditions are as follows:

$${c}_{p,w}^{m}\ge {c}_{w}^{m* },\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}},\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w},$$

(9)

$${f}_{p,w}^{m}({c}_{p,w}^{m}-{c}_{w}^{m* })=0,\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}},\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}.$$

(10)

Equation (10) is the pure UE condition. Introducing ξm, a parameter that converts time in hours to cost in euros, the total travel time cost of the system is:

$${J}_{1}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{m\in {\mathcal{M}}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{w\in {\mathcal{W}}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}}{f}_{p,w}^{m}{c}_{p,w}^{m}{\xi }^{m},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}},\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}.$$

(11)

In the classical SO formulation, the decision variables are path or link flows, and the objective is to minimise the total system travel time, without requiring the flows to satisfy UE conditions. In contrast, in our formulation, we always keep either UE or BRUE constraints in the feasible set, and then minimise a system-level objective (total travel time, or total travel time plus emissions) over that behaviourally feasible set. Thus, when we later refer to “SO”, “UE-SOTT” or “BRUE-SOTT”, this denotes a system-optimal objective evaluated over UE- or BRUE-consistent flows (a behaviourally constrained system optimum), rather than a free, unconstrained SO.

Alternatively, the User Equilibrium problem can be expressed as an optimization problem over link flows, originally formulated by ref. 61. This link-based formulation is useful for analyzing the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium:

$$\begin{array}{l}\mathop{\min }\limits_{x}\,\mathop{\sum }\limits_{e\in {\mathcal{E}}}{\int }_{0}^{{x}_{e}}{c}_{e}(s)\,ds\\ \,{\rm{s.t.}}\,\,\,{\rm{Link\; -\; path\; flow\; conservation\; and\; non\; -\; negativity\; constraints.}}\end{array}$$

(12)

Here, xe is the total flow on link e, and ce(xe) is the travel cost (or time) on link e, assumed to be continuous and strictly increasing. This objective function is strictly convex under such assumptions, ensuring a unique solution to the UE problem.

Bounded rationality

The Bounded Rationality User Equilibrium (BRUE) approach relaxes the UE by introducing an indifference band, allowing travelers to accept routes with costs within this band of the minimum cost. Consequently, several routes with similar travel times become equally attractive, resulting in non-unique solutions. Travelers may choose various routes within this band based on personal preferences. For a given OD pair, the path flow depends on the value of the indifference parameter.

In this work, we interpret the indifference band as a relative tolerance on perceived route cost. Specifically, we introduce a scalar parameter ϵ ∈ (0, 1), common to all vehicle classes and OD pairs, and for each class m and OD pair w we define an absolute tolerance

$${\epsilon }_{w}^{m}:=\epsilon \,{c}_{w}^{m* },$$

where \({c}_{w}^{m* }\) is the minimum generalised cost between w for class m. A path is then considered acceptable for users of class m if its cost is within a fraction ϵ of the minimum cost.

A feasible path flow vector adheres to the ϵ-BRUE criteria if users select any route whose cost remains within this tolerance of the shortest path62. Therefore, in our multi-class study:

$$\begin{array}{cc}({f}_{p,w}^{m} > 0)\Rightarrow {c}_{p,w}^{m}-{c}_{w}^{m* }\le {\epsilon }_{w}^{m}, & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}},\,\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}.\end{array}\,$$

(13)

This flexibility expands the solution space, changing the equilibrium from a point to a region.

Later, a linearized version of equation (13) will be presented for implementation under different scenarios.

Emission model

While travel time has been addressed with a complex model, our second objective is minimizing the network’s total emissions. Emissions are established at the link level, dependent on the class m link flow \({x}_{e}^{m}\) is given by:

$${J}_{2}=\theta \mathop{\sum }\limits_{m\in {\mathcal{M}}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{e\in {\mathcal{E}}}{E}_{e}^{m}{x}_{e}^{m},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(14)

where,

$${E}_{e}^{m}=E{F}_{e}^{m}({v}_{e}^{m}){L}_{e},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(15)

$$E{F}_{e}^{m}={a}_{e,1}^{m}{({v}_{e}^{m})}^{-1}+{a}_{e,2}^{m}+{a}_{e,3}^{m}{v}_{e}^{m}+{a}_{e,4}^{m}{({v}_{e}^{m})}^{2},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(16)

$${v}_{e}^{m}=\frac{{L}_{e}}{{c}_{e}^{m}},\,{\rm{speed\; on\; link}}\,\,e\,{\rm{for\; class}}\,\,m,\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(17)

$${E}_{e}^{m}({c}_{e}^{m})=E{F}_{e}^{m}{L}_{e},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(18)

Here, θ = 70 € /ton CO2 emission63, converts emission to euros, making J2 an emission cost, similar to how J1 is a time cost, and both are strictly monotonic functions. The total cost of the system is the sum of these two components. Equation (16) is derived from the emission models used by ref. 44, which in turn are based on ref. 35 and ref. 64. The emission factors for light-duty (class 1) vehicles and heavy-duty (class 2) vehicles (g/km), are listed below, where V denotes the speed value:

$$E{F}_{{\rm{light}}}=4.78\times 1{0}^{3}\times {V}^{-1}+1.11\times 1{0}^{2}-1.24\times V+2.37\times 1{0}^{-2}\times {V}^{2}$$

(19)

$$E{F}_{{\rm{heavy}}}=3.67\times 1{0}^{3}\times {V}^{-1}+5.34\times 1{0}^{2}-7.90\times V+5.43\times 1{0}^{-2}\times {V}^{2}$$

(20)

These equations are used in the programming process and are crucial for calculating emissions and evaluating the overall model’s effectiveness. However, as presented, they can be quite complex, and linearization is needed to simplify the model. The emission factors implement a mesoscopic average-speed relationship, in which CO2 emissions are represented as a function of link-average speed for two aggregate vehicle classes (passenger cars and heavy-duty trucks). This formulation is intended for planning-level comparisons of speed-limit and assignment policies under static equilibrium assumptions. It does not explicitly capture vehicle operating modes (idling, acceleration, braking), stop-and-go dynamics, road grade, vehicle-specific power, cold-start effects, nor fleet heterogeneity such as vehicle age, engine technology class (e.g., Euro standards), fuel type, or load/commodity characteristics. Consequently, the absolute magnitude of predicted emissions should be interpreted as relative differences between scenarios computed under consistent assumptions.

Speed control

In the previous subsections, we introduced the multi-class traffic assignment problem under UE and BRUE conditions, assuming given (exogenous) free-flow speeds \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\) and corresponding free-flow travel times \({T}_{e}^{m}={L}_{e}/{v}_{e,0}^{m}\). In this subsection, we extend the formulation by introducing speed control as an additional decision layer. The idea is to treat free-flow speeds (or, equivalently, speed limits) as controllable variables that can be adjusted on each link and for each vehicle class within admissible ranges, in order to improve the overall system performance in terms of travel time and emissions.

Let \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\) denote the free-flow speed of class \(m\in {\mathcal{M}}\) on link \(e\in {\mathcal{E}}\). In the speed control (SC) models, these variables are no longer fixed, but are instead chosen by the optimisation subject to lower and upper bounds:

$${v}_{e,0}^{m-}\le {v}_{e,0}^{m}\le {v}_{e,0}^{m+},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(21)

where \({v}_{e,0}^{m-}\) and \({v}_{e,0}^{m+}\) represent, respectively, the minimum and maximum admissible free-flow speeds (e.g., reflecting lower and upper speed limits for each vehicle class on each link).

Given the free-flow speed \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\), the associated free-flow travel time on link e for class m is

$${T}_{e}^{m}=\frac{{L}_{e}}{{v}_{e,0}^{m}},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(22)

In the presence of congestion, travel times are still modeled via a BPR-type volume-delay function. For convenience, we rewrite the expression in a form that is particularly useful for the SC formulation:

$${c}_{e}^{m}{v}_{e,0}^{m}={L}_{e}\left(1+\alpha {\left(\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m}^{{\prime} }\in {\mathcal{M}}}\frac{{x}_{e}^{{m}^{{\prime} }}{\pi }^{{m}^{{\prime} }}}{{K}_{e}}\right)}^{\beta }\right)=:{f}_{e}({x}_{e}),\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(23)

where \({x}_{e}={\sum }_{m\in {\mathcal{M}}}{x}_{e}^{m}{\pi }^{m}\) is the total (PCE-weighted) flow on link e, and fe(xe) denotes the corresponding volume-delay term. Equation (23) highlights the coupling between link travel time \({c}_{e}^{m}\) and free-flow speed \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\) through the product \({c}_{e}^{m}{v}_{e,0}^{m}\).

In the SC variants of our models, the decision variables therefore consist of:

path flows \({f}_{p,w}^{m}\), and the induced link flows \({x}_{e}^{m}\),

UE or BRUE equilibrium-consistency variables (e.g., the path-flow variables entering (9), (10) and (13)),

free-flow speeds \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\) on each link and for each class.

The objective is to minimise a system-level function (total travel time, or total travel time plus emissions) subject to:

flow conservation constraints (1)–(4),

UE equilibrium constraints (9)–(10) or BRUE equilibrium constraint (13),

the BPR-based speed-flow relation (23),

the admissible bounds on free-flow speeds (21).

In the numerical experiments, the SC models correspond to the scenarios labelled SC-UE-SOTT+E and SC-BRUE-SOTT+E, where both route choice and free-flow speeds are optimised under UE or BRUE behavioural constraints. The following subsections describe how these nonlinear relations are linearised and embedded into a MILP formulation.

Emission linearization

To implement the emission model in a MILP framework, we first linearise the nonlinear functions involved in the emission computation, namely the dependence of emissions on travel time (via speed). As described in Section Emission model, emissions on link e for class m are given by

$${E}_{e}^{m}=E{F}_{e}^{m}({v}_{e}^{m}){L}_{e},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(24)

$$E{F}_{e}^{m}({v}_{e}^{m})={a}_{e,1}^{m}{({v}_{e}^{m})}^{-1}+{a}_{e,2}^{m}+{a}_{e,3}^{m}{v}_{e}^{m}+{a}_{e,4}^{m}{({v}_{e}^{m})}^{2},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(25)

$${v}_{e}^{m}=\frac{{L}_{e}}{{c}_{e}^{m}},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(26)

Combining these expressions shows that emissions \({E}_{e}^{m}\) are nonlinear functions of the link travel time \({c}_{e}^{m}\). To approximate this dependence, we use Special Ordered Set Type 2 (SOS2) constraints, which are commonly used to construct efficient piecewise linear approximations of nonlinear functions in MILP models.

Let l index the breakpoints of the piecewise approximation, with l ∈ {1, 2, …, L + 1}, where L is the number of segments. For each link e and class m, we define:

\({c}_{e,l}^{m}\): the value of the travel time at breakpoint l,

\({\eta }_{e,l}^{m}\in [0,1]\): the SOS2 weights associated with these breakpoints.

The SOS2 constraints are then:

$$\,{\rm{SOS2\; :}}\,[({\eta }_{e,1}^{m},{c}_{e,1}^{m}),\ldots ,({\eta }_{e,L+1}^{m},{c}_{e,L+1}^{m})],\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(27)

$${\eta }_{e,l}^{m}\in [0,1],\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},\,\forall l\in \{1,\ldots ,L+1\},$$

(28)

$$\mathop{\sum }\limits_{l=1}^{L+1}{\eta }_{e,l}^{m}=1,\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(29)

$$\mathop{\sum }\limits_{l=1}^{L+1}{\eta }_{e,l}^{m}{c}_{e,l}^{m}={c}_{e}^{m},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(30)

The SOS2 structure ensures that, for each pair (e, m), at most two adjacent \({\eta }_{e,l}^{m}\) can be nonzero, and they must sum to one. This yields a convex combination of two neighbouring breakpoints, providing a continuous, piecewise-linear approximation of \({c}_{e}^{m}\).

Using the same weights, we approximate the emission function \({E}_{e}^{m}({c}_{e}^{m})\) as:

$${\overline{E}}_{e}^{m}({c}_{e}^{m})=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{l=1}^{L+1}{E}_{e}^{m}({c}_{e,l}^{m})\,{\eta }_{e,l}^{m},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(31)

where \({E}_{e}^{m}({c}_{e,l}^{m})\) is the emission value computed from (24)–(26) at the breakpoint \({c}_{e,l}^{m}\). The quantity \({\overline{E}}_{e}^{m}({c}_{e}^{m})\) is then used in place of \({E}_{e}^{m}\) in the objective function and in the computation of J2:

$${J}_{2}=\theta \mathop{\sum }\limits_{m\in {\mathcal{M}}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{e\in {\mathcal{E}}}{\overline{E}}_{e}^{m}({c}_{e}^{m})\,{x}_{e}^{m}.$$

(32)

This yields a linear expression in the decision variables and SOS2 weights, while retaining a close approximation of the original nonlinear emission model.

Speed control linearization

We now describe how the speed control model introduced in the previous section is linearised and incorporated into the MILP formulation. The key nonlinearities arise from:

the BPR-type volume-delay function fe(xe),

the product of travel time \({c}_{e}^{m}\) and free-flow speed \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\) in (23).

Recall that the continuous BPR relation with speed control can be written as:

$${c}_{e}^{m}{v}_{e,0}^{m}={L}_{e}\left(1+\alpha {\left(\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m}^{{\prime} }\in {\mathcal{M}}}\frac{{x}_{e}^{{m}^{{\prime} }}{\pi }^{{m}^{{\prime} }}}{{K}_{e}}\right)}^{\beta }\right)={f}_{e}({x}_{e}),\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(33)

To obtain a tractable linear model, we proceed in two steps.

(i) Bounding the product using speed limits:

Using the bounds \({v}_{e,0}^{m-}\le {v}_{e,0}^{m}\le {v}_{e,0}^{m+}\), we first write:

$${c}_{e}^{m}{v}_{e,0}^{m-}\le {f}_{e}({x}_{e}),\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(34)

$${c}_{e}^{m}{v}_{e,0}^{m+}\ge {f}_{e}({x}_{e}),\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(35)

These inequalities ensure that the feasible region in the \(({c}_{e}^{m},{v}_{e,0}^{m})\)-space is constrained so that the product \({c}_{e}^{m}{v}_{e,0}^{m}\) lies in an interval containing the nonlinear term fe(xe) for each link and class. Once fe(xe) itself is approximated via a piecewise linear function, (34), (35) can be expressed with linear constraints.

(ii) Piecewise linear approximation of the volume-delay function:

Let L = Lleft + Lright denote the total number of segments in the piecewise approximation of the BPR function as a function of total link flow xe. For each link e, we define a set of breakpoints on the flow domain:

$${\widetilde{x}}_{e,l}=\frac{{K}_{e}}{{L}_{{\rm{left}}}}(l-1),\,l=1,2,\ldots ,L+1,$$

and introduce continuous SOS2 weights \({b}_{e,l}^{m}\in [0,1]\). The SOS2 constraints on these variables are:

$$\left[({b}_{e,1}^{m},0),({b}_{e,2}^{m},\frac{{K}_{e}}{{L}_{{\rm{left}}}}),\ldots ,({b}_{e,L+1}^{m},\frac{{K}_{e}}{{L}_{{\rm{left}}}}\times L)\right],\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(36)

$$\mathop{\sum }\limits_{l=1}^{L+1}{b}_{e,l}^{m}=1,\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(37)

$$\mathop{\sum }\limits_{l=1}^{L+1}{b}_{e,l}^{m}\left(\frac{{K}_{e}}{{L}_{{\rm{left}}}}(l-1)\right)={x}_{e},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(38)

We then approximate the volume-delay term as:

$$\mathop{\sum }\limits_{l=1}^{L+1}{b}_{e,l}^{m}\,{f}_{e}\,\left(\frac{{K}_{e}}{{L}_{\mathrm{left}}}(l-1)\right)\ge {\widehat{c}}_{e}^{m}{v}_{e,0}^{m-},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}},$$

(39)

$$\mathop{\sum }\limits_{l=1}^{L+1}{b}_{e,l}^{m}\,{f}_{e}\,\left(\frac{{K}_{e}}{{L}_{\mathrm{left}}}(l-1)\right)\le {\widehat{c}}_{e}^{m}{v}_{e,0}^{m+},\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall e\in {\mathcal{E}}.$$

(40)

Here, \({\hat{c}}_{e}^{m}\) denotes the travel time variable appearing in the linearised BPR formulation for class m on link e. Equations (39)–(40), combined with (34)–(35), ensure that the approximate travel times \({\hat{c}}_{e}^{m}\) are consistent with both:

the piecewise linear approximation of the BPR function fe(xe),

the admissible range of free-flow speeds \([{v}_{e,0}^{m-},{v}_{e,0}^{m+}]\).

BRUE linearization

To linearise the BRUE implication in (13), we introduce a binary variable \({a}_{p,w}^{m}\) indicating whether path p is used for OD pair w and class m:

$${a}_{p,w}^{m}=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}0, & \,{\rm{if}}\,{f}_{p,w}^{m}=0,\\ 1, & \,{\rm{if}}\,{f}_{p,w}^{m} > 0,\end{array}\right.\,\forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}},\,\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}.$$

(41)

Using the big-M method, the BRUE condition (13),

$$({f}_{p,w}^{m} > 0)\Rightarrow {c}_{p,w}^{m}-{c}_{w}^{m* }\le {\epsilon }_{w}^{m},$$

is enforced by the following pair of linear constraints:

$$\begin{array}{cc}{c}_{p,w}^{m}-{c}_{w}^{m* }\le {\epsilon }_{w}^{m}+M(1-{a}_{p,w}^{m}), & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}},\,\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w},\end{array}\,$$

(42)

$$\begin{array}{cc}0\le {f}_{p,w}^{m}\le {d}_{w}^{m}{a}_{p,w}^{m}, & \forall m\in {\mathcal{M}},\,\forall w\in {\mathcal{W}},\,\forall p\in {{\mathcal{P}}}_{w}.\end{array}\,$$

(43)

Here, M is a sufficiently large positive constant. Constraint (43) links the binary path-use variable and the continuous path-flow variable: if \({a}_{p,w}^{m}=0\), then \({f}_{p,w}^{m}=0\), while any positive path flow requires \({a}_{p,w}^{m}=1\). Therefore, for every used path, constraint (42) reduces to \({c}_{p,w}^{m}-{c}_{w}^{m* }\le {\epsilon }_{w}^{m}\), which is the BRUE tolerance condition. For unused paths, the big-M term relaxes the tolerance constraint, so unused paths are not required to lie within the indifference band.

Together with the emission-linearisation constraints in previous section and the UE/BRUE equilibrium constraints, the above approximations yield a mixed-integer linear programming formulation in which path flows, link flows and free-flow speeds are decision variables, travel times and emissions are approximated via SOS2-based piecewise linear functions, and speed control is explicitly represented through the variables \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\) and constraints (34)–(40).

This linearised SC formulation is then used in the scenarios labeled SC-UE-SOTT+E and SC-BRUE-SOTT+E in the numerical experiments, where a behaviourally constrained system optimum is computed under explicit, link-specific speed regulation.

MILP formulation

With the development of the MILP model, we now present the final linearized formulation in which a system-level objective (total travel time plus emissions) is minimised subject to UE or BRUE constraints. As discussed above, this corresponds to a behaviourally constrained system optimum (UE- or BRUE-consistent SO), not a classical unconstrained SO.

The objective is to determine the traffic flow that optimizes the problem under the given constraints. Achieving this solution will provide insights into the flow distribution that aligns with environmental goals. Implementing the overall model and conducting numerical experiments are essential to achieving this objective.

Solution uniqueness

The uniqueness properties of traffic assignment models are critical to understanding the implications of any optimization solution. In the context of our MILP formulation for the UE and BRUE problems, it is important to distinguish between the uniqueness of link flows and path flows.

The role of multiple vehicle classes is especially relevant here. In multi-class traffic assignment, users of different vehicle types (e.g., cars and trucks) perceive costs differently due to factors such as vehicle size, speed sensitivity, and emission intensity. These class-based differences are embedded into the cost functions and demand profiles, shaping the equilibrium outcomes. Importantly, while multi-class UE still yields a unique solution at the link level under monotonic cost functions, the presence of multiple vehicle classes increases the complexity and dimensionality of the solution space at the path level, reinforcing its non-uniqueness. This study utilizes this structure by applying system-optimal objectives, minimizing total travel time and emissions, within the space of path flow distributions that are consistent with the unique multi-class UE link flows. The link-level equilibrium is preserved to reflect user-consistent behavior, while the optimization identifies the most efficient path flow configuration from a system perspective. This hybrid formulation allows us to maintain behavioral realism while improving environmental and operational performance. We refer to such solutions as behaviourally constrained system optima (UE-consistent or BRUE-consistent SO), and this is the notion of “SO” used throughout the numerical experiments.

The classical UE problem can be formulated as a convex minimization program over link flows, often attributed to ref. 61. This formulation minimizes total system travel cost subject to flow conservation constraints. When cost functions are continuous and strictly increasing (as in our linearized BPR functions), the objective function is strictly convex. Given the convexity of the objective and the linearity of constraints, this formulation yields a unique solution in terms of link flows xe, even in the multi-class case. Thus, under our MILP assumptions with fixed demand and monotonic cost functions, the link flow solution is unique.

While link flows are unique, the corresponding path flows are not. Multiple path flow distributions can yield the same aggregate link flows. For each OD pair \(w\in {\mathcal{W}}\) and vehicle class \(m\in {\mathcal{M}}\), the path flows \({f}_{p,w}^{m}\) must satisfy demand and flow conservation constraints (Equations (3) and (4)). Due to the linearity of these constraints, an infinite number of feasible path flow configurations (or a finite number in the MILP setting) can generate the same unique link-level solution. This path-level flexibility is particularly pronounced in multi-class models, where distinct vehicle classes may share links but differ in route cost perception. Consequently, path-flow solutions are more variable in multi-class settings than in single-class settings.

This distinction has direct implications for transportation policy and network management. While link-level strategies (e.g., pricing or speed control) can be designed based on the unique link flows, path-level interventions (such as route guidance or incentives) must account for the variability in feasible path assignments. In BRUE models, where users accept near-optimal routes, this flexibility is amplified, better aligning with real-world behaviors.

The MILP formulation enhances behavioral and operational realism by incorporating piecewise-linear approximations of travel time and emission functions, as well as logical constraints (e.g., SOS2 and BRUE tolerance bands). A key benefit is that it reduces the infinite path flow solution space to a finite set of feasible configurations, enabling tractable optimization.

Furthermore, the joint minimization of total travel time (J1) and emissions (J2), both monotonic functions, guides the solution toward system-optimal behavior while respecting user equilibrium at the link level. Since these objectives both depend on aggregate link usage, path flow differences among optimal solutions tend to be minor. As a result, while multiple path configurations may exist, their policy impact remains limited, and the MILP provides a robust, interpretable framework for evaluating low-emission traffic management strategies.

Model scenarios

This section applies the methodology to a freeway network in Tilburg, The Netherlands, consisting of 18 nodes and 44 links, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Various scenarios are analyzed under User Equilibrium (UE) and Bounded Rationality User Equilibrium (BRUE) constraints. Initially, only path flow is considered as a decision variable, followed by the inclusion of free-flow speed. Speed limits for cars vary within the range of [ − 30%; + 15%], while for trucks, the range is [ − 20%; + 10%]. The network and vehicle demand data are sourced from the Dutch National Model System (Landelijke Model System, LMS,vRijkswaterstaat, 2012).

The mathematical model has been implemented in MATLAB and Python, executed using the GUROBI optimization solver. For the data and code, please refer to the data availability statement section. The bi-objective function is scalarised by expressing both travel time and emissions in monetary units and minimizing their sum J1 + J2. The nonlinear BPR travel-time functions and the link emission functions are approximated by piecewise-linear functions using SOS2 constraints, so that the final problem has a linear objective and linear constraints with a mixed-integer structure.

We consider optimizing J1 + J2, and as discussed earlier, the joint optimization of these objectives under UE conditions tends to yield solutions similar to the UE-consistent behaviourally constrained SO. Supporting numerical evidence is provided in Supplementary Figure S1 and Supplementary Tables S1, S2, and S3. However, for the BRUE setting, we present all the variations in the objective function, as it leads to different solutions. This is due to the flexibility embedded in the BRUE formulation, which allows users to choose routes within an indifference band rather than strictly minimizing travel time. As a result, the solution space under BRUE is significantly larger than under UE, and even small changes in the objective function can lead to noticeably different link and path flow patterns. As summarized in Table 4 below, multiple scenarios under different equilibria are considered. The models with subscript TT+E optimize the scalarized combined objective J1 + J2, in which travel time and emissions are both expressed in monetary units. An SC (Speed Control) model incorporates free-flow speed directly as a decision variable in the optimization process.

In scenarios labeled SOTT or SOTT+E, the model explores the set of feasible path-flow distributions that are consistent with the UE or BRUE constraints for the corresponding scenario. SOTT denotes a behaviourally constrained system optimum with respect to total travel time, while SOTT+E denotes a behaviourally constrained system optimum with respect to the scalarized combined travel-time and emission-cost objective J1 + J2. The subscript TT+E therefore does not denote an emission-only objective. In all cases, the objective is optimized within the corresponding equilibrium-feasible set, rather than as a classical unconstrained system optimum.

No emission-only scenario is included in the main comparison. This is intentional: the policy problem considered here is not to minimize emissions at any travel-time cost, but to evaluate behaviourally feasible traffic-management strategies using a scalarized economic objective in which travel time and emissions are both monetized. Emission-only optimization could be studied as an extreme sensitivity case, but it would represent a different policy question and is left for future work.

For the UE family, the travel-time-only and combined-objective behaviourally constrained optima coincide in the Tilburg experiment; therefore, only UE-SOTT+E is reported in the main comparison, while the equivalence with UE-SOTT is documented in Supplementary Figure S1 and Supplementary Tables S1–S3. For the BRUE family, the indifference band enlarges the feasible path-flow region, so BRUE-SOTT and BRUE-SOTT+E may lead to different flow distributions and are both included in the main analysis.

The flow is determined at the link level to calculate emissions. The primary goal is to assess whether incorporating freeflow speed as a decision variable (DV) improves the model by minimizing emissions and total costs. Additionally, evaluating the impact of introducing flexibility by transitioning from a UE model to a BRUE model is of significant interest. By exploring the model presented in the previous chapter through various scenarios, this study aims to contribute to the development of traffic management systems that are both eco-friendly and economically viable, paving the way for smarter and more sustainable urban mobility solutions.

Overall comparison

In this section, all seven scenarios are reviewed and compared. The pure UE scenario differs significantly from UE-SOTT+E, with distinct TTT and emission values. This clearly illustrates the non-uniqueness of solutions in multi-class TAP under UE assumptions, where multiple path flow configurations can satisfy the equilibrium conditions. While the total link flows may appear identical across certain scenarios, differences in class-specific path flow distributions can influence emission and performance metrics, particularly under BRUE, where the relaxed rationality condition permits a broader solution space.

The results show that the effect of BRUE depends on the system objective and the available feasible path-flow region. Relative to the pure UE baseline, the pure BRUE scenario slightly reduces total travel time, from 6.46 to 6.30 million hours, but slightly increases modeled emissions, from 30.8 to 31.3 thousand kg. When a travel-time objective is imposed within the BRUE-feasible set, BRUE-SOTT yields the lowest total travel time among the Tilburg scenarios, at 4.94 million hours. When the scalarized travel-time and emission-cost objective is used, BRUE-SOTT+E reduces modeled emissions relative to pure BRUE, while keeping total travel time below the pure UE baseline.

Adding speed control further reduces modeled emissions. In particular, SC-BRUE-SOTT+E gives the lowest modeled emissions among all Tilburg scenarios. Compared with BRUE-SOTT+E, SC-BRUE-SOTT+E reduces modeled emissions by 16.2%, while increasing total travel time by 6.0%. These results indicate that the main environmental gain in the Tilburg case comes from combining bounded-rational route flexibility with speed control, while the magnitude of the emission reduction should be interpreted within the static average-speed emission framework adopted in this paper.

These results not only highlight the value of flexibility in route choice but also demonstrate how integrating speed control within the optimization provides a robust framework for designing planning-level speed regulation policies over successive planning horizons, effectively steering the network toward more sustainable operational states.

Similar observations apply to time and emission costs. This study uses θ = 70 €/ton CO2 and ξ1 = 9, ξ2 = 38€/h63, enabling to obtain the costs in Table 6.

Focusing only on emission savings, scenarios that incorporate speed as a decision variable, particularly SC-UE-SOTT+E and SC-BRUE-SOTT+E, are most advantageous, achieving significant reductions in emission costs. Generally, adding free-flow speed (dependent on speed limits) as a decision variable reduces emissions but increases total travel time, as previously noted. Conversely, if minimizing total travel time and achieving system optimum is the priority, BRUE-SOTT stands out, with a time cost of 7.3815e+07€.

Considering the total cost, which includes both time and emission costs, BRUE-SOTT offers the greatest savings. Although it does not minimize emissions as effectively as SC-BRUE-SOTT+E, it provides the most balanced flow distribution to minimize overall costs. Within the static average-speed emission framework adopted in this paper, SC-BRUE-SOTT+E reduces modeled emissions by 26% relative to the pure UE baseline and by 27% relative to the pure BRUE baseline, while maintaining a relatively small increase in total passenger travel cost and achieving over 10% savings in truck costs.

The emission values in Tables 5 and 6 should be interpreted as model-internal estimates obtained with the static average-speed emission kernel in equations (19) and (20). Operating-mode-aware or fleet-composition-aware emission estimators may rescale the absolute magnitudes and percentage reductions, although the present results remain useful for comparing scenarios under consistent assumptions.

The next section will provide a more detailed analysis of the results, distinguishing between models with a single decision variable, which is flow (route choice), and SC-based models that also integrate speed as a decision variable.

Flow-only optimization

This section explores scenarios where flow is the only decision variable: UE, UE-SOTT+E, BRUE, and BRUE-SOTT+E. For each link and mode, an average speed has been calculated to determine emissions accordingly. The volume of vehicles and corresponding emissions are obtained, with speed limits represented as dotted lines.

Figure 3 presents the volume and CO2 emissions of cars and trucks as a function of their average speed for the UE and UE-SOTT+E scenarios. Panel a shows the UE scenario, while panel b shows the UE-SOTT+E scenario. In the UE scenario (Fig. 3a), the majority of trucks are concentrated at higher speeds between 60 and 90 km/h, where emissions remain moderate. Cars, however, are spread more widely across the speed range, with a significant volume still present at both very low speeds(e.g., 10-20 km/h) and high speeds (e.g., 130-140 km/h), leading to peaks in emissions at both ends of the speed spectrum. This uneven distribution suggests inefficiencies in both emissions and possibly travel time. In contrast, Fig. 3b shows the results for the UE-SOTT+E scenario. Here, both cars and trucks exhibit a more concentrated volume between 50 and 90 km/h, which aligns with speed ranges that balance travel time and emissions more effectively. This reflects a more efficient and environmentally favorable distribution. Comparing the two graphs in Fig. 3, the maximum and minimum emissions under UE-SOTT+E are lower than those of UE.

Figure 4 displays the volume and CO2 emissions under the BRUE scenario, where route choice flexibility is introduced through an indifference band (ϵ = 10%). In this case, car volumes are highly concentrated around a speed of 84 km/h, with nearly 14,000 vehicles operating in this efficient range. This coincides with a local emission minimum for cars, indicating that many drivers are shifting toward emission-optimal speeds. Unlike the UE case, very few cars operate at extreme low or high speeds, reducing peaks in emissions. For trucks, the volume is distributed more broadly but still largely concentrated between 50 and 85 km/h, suggesting a balanced approach between minimizing emissions and maintaining reasonable travel times. Truck emissions are mostly kept below 0.5 kg/km, showing improved environmental performance compared to the UE scenario. This outcome demonstrates how BRUE enables more environmentally and operationally efficient route choices through bounded rationality.

Figure 5 compares the BRUE-SOTT and BRUE-SOTT+E scenarios. In panel a, corresponding to BRUE-SOTT, both cars and trucks tend to operate at higher speeds than in the pure BRUE scenario, since the objective prioritizes total travel-time minimization. Vehicle volumes are therefore concentrated close to the respective free-flow speed limits.

In panel b, corresponding to BRUE-SOTT+E, the distribution shifts toward more emission-efficient speeds, especially for cars. As speed increases, car volumes gradually decrease, while a substantial share of cars, nearly one-third of the total car flow (13,898 vehicles), is concentrated at 84 km/h. This speed represents about 56% of the car speed limit and corresponds to one of the lowest emission levels. The combined travel-time and emission-cost objective therefore redirects traffic toward operating conditions that are more favorable from an emissions perspective.

These results highlight how introducing flexibility in route choice can yield different benefits depending on the optimization goal. BRUE-SOTT achieves the best performance in terms of travel time, while BRUE-SOTT+E delivers the lowest emissions, without significantly sacrificing time efficiency. Such trade-offs underline the importance of considering multiple objectives in traffic planning.

Speed control results

In this subsection, we examine the effects of incorporating free-flow speed as a decision variable alongside traffic flow. The free-flow speed is determined by speed limits, constrained as \({v}_{e,0}^{m}\in [{v}_{e,0}^{m-},{v}_{e,0}^{m+}]\) where \({v}_{e,0}^{m-}\) and \({v}_{e,0}^{m+}\) represent the range of allowable speeds. Our focus shifts to scenarios in which the scalarized combined objective J1 + J2 is optimized with free-flow speed included as an additional decision variable.

Figure 6 illustrates the traffic volume and emissions under the SC-UE-SOTT+E scenario, where both traffic flow and free-flow speeds are decision variables. This scenario jointly optimizes traffic flow and free-flow speeds under UE constraints. Trucks follow a relatively consistent pattern as observed in earlier scenarios, with a concentration between 50 and 80 km/h. Their speeds remain moderate and emissions relatively low.

Cars, on the other hand, show a notable concentration at two distinct speeds: a medium band between 30 and 70 km/h, and a sharp peak at 84 km/h (near the free-flow speed limit). Notably, 16,650 cars operate at this optimized speed, which has a low emission rate of 0.3 kg/km, demonstrating the system’s ability to consolidate flow at emission-efficient speeds. Compared to previous UE-only models, this scenario demonstrates that incorporating speed control significantly enhances environmental performance. High-speed outliers, like those above 120 km/h (which were present in UE scenarios), are now completely eliminated. This results in a more emission-efficient and streamlined distribution of traffic volumes, especially for cars.

The next set of results assesses the effects of speed control under bounded rationality. The results of the SC-BRUE-SOTT and SC-BRUE-SOTT+E models are shown in panels a and b of Fig. 7, respectively. Although SC-BRUE-SOTT+E outperforms SC-BRUE-SOTT in terms of the scalarized combined objective, the two panels show highly similar traffic and emission distributions. This indicates that adding the emission-cost component to the travel-time objective does not substantially alter the speed and flow patterns in the speed-control BRUE setting.

In both scenarios, car volumes peak at around 84 km/h with over 13,000 vehicles, a speed that aligns with one of the lowest CO2 emission levels. This confirms that medium-range speeds (approximately 50–90 km/h) are optimal for balancing emissions and efficiency. Notably, in both SC-BRUE-SOTT and SC-BRUE-SOTT+E, car speeds are tightly clustered in this optimal range, with no cars traveling faster than 94 km/h, effectively avoiding the higher emissions seen at extreme speeds in previous scenarios. Truck volumes also show consistency between the two cases, with the majority operating below 65 km/h. Although these speeds are slightly lower than those observed in BRUE-SOTT (Fig. 5), they remain within an environmentally favorable range.

Compared to the UE-based scenarios (e.g., Fig. 6), the SC BRUE solution demonstrates a much tighter distribution around emission-optimal speeds. This confirms the effectiveness of combining route flexibility with speed control for reducing environmental impact. However, this reduction in emissions comes with the trade-off of longer travel times, as discussed in Tables 5 and 6.

Finally, we examine the sensitivity of the BRUE-based scenarios to the choice of the indifference parameter ϵ, which governs travellers’ tolerance for suboptimal paths. Recall that ϵ is interpreted as a relative tolerance on perceived route cost and is implemented as a single scalar applied uniformly to all vehicle classes and OD pairs (see BRUE subsection). For a given value of ϵ, the corresponding absolute tolerance \({\epsilon }_{w}^{m}=\epsilon \,{c}_{w}^{m* }\) is therefore class- and OD-specific, but generated from the same underlying relative band.

Figure 8 displays the total system cost (in euros) under three different indifference levels: ϵ = 5%, 10%, and 15%. The results indicate a modest but steady decline in total cost as ϵ increases. While the difference between 5% and 10% is relatively small, the 15% case yields a more noticeable cost reduction, reflecting the fact that a wider indifference band allows the BRUE formulation to exploit a larger set of near-equilibrium path-flow configurations.

Overall, this analysis supports the use of a ϵ = 10% indifference band in the main experiments: it provides enough flexibility for BRUE to improve system performance relative to UE, while remaining consistent with a behavioural assumption that travellers accept routes whose generalised cost is within a limited percentage of the best available alternative. The 15% case suggests that additional savings are possible under more tolerant behaviour, but such large bands may be less realistic for some user groups. A richer specification with class-dependent indifference bands ϵm could capture these differences, but would require additional behavioural data, and is left for future work.

Melbourne case study

To complement the Tilburg analysis and assess large-scale generalizability, we apply the proposed multi-class equilibrium and speed-control formulations to a metropolitan freeway test case derived from the Melbourne GMNS network65. The network is presented in Fig. 9. For the data and code, please refer to the data availability statement section. All scenarios were solved with Gurobi Optimizer 13.0.1 under identical settings (time limit 1800 s per scenario, 14 threads) on Apple M4 Pro hardware.

The truck demand share is fixed to 15%, chosen as a representative heavy-vehicle proportion for metropolitan freeway links (https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/historical-annual-average-daily-traffic-volume). Speed-control bounds follow the model definitions used in the previous use case (cars: [ − 30%, + 15%], trucks: [ − 20%, + 10%] around class-specific free-flow speed limits). Table 7 reports the main case characteristics after path-based reduction.

We compare seven policy scenarios as defined in Table 4, which isolate the marginal contributions of (i) bounded-rational route flexibility (BRUE) and (ii) network-wide speed control (SC), under a consistent multi-class objective structure and identical solution settings. This Melbourne experiment is full-scale in network size, but selective in the optimization layer: while assignment and performance evaluation are carried out for the full demand matrix, the control and optimization problem acts on a truncated set of high-demand OD pairs (i.e., OD pairs with the greatest demand), capturing the most influential movements in the network. As reported in Table 7, the MILP optimizes flows for 340 OD pairs (cars and trucks), representing 42,036 vehicles, i.e., 12.5% of the total demand. This design reflects a realistic operational setting in which a controller targets a limited set of influential OD movements and controllable freeway links (here, 2146 speed-controllable road links) rather than requiring complete OD observability or full OD-level actuation.

Table 8 reports travel-time and emissions outcomes by class. Despite optimizing only 12.5% of OD demand, the speed-control scenarios deliver network-wide improvements relative to the UE baseline. In particular, SC-UE-SOTT+E reduces total travel time by 11.70% (from 43,269 h to 38,206 h) and total emissions by 2.55% (from 292.06 to 284.60 ton CO2e). Similarly, SC-BRUE-SOTT+E reduces total travel time by 11.34% and total emissions by 2.02%. These results indicate that, across this large freeway system, strategically adjusting free-flow speeds and controlling speeds on 2146 speed-controllable road links can reshape congestion patterns sufficiently to generate aggregate travel-time gains, while also shifting operating speeds into lower-emission regimes, yielding simultaneous efficiency and environmental benefits.

By contrast, BRUE without speed control is slightly worse than UE in this instance (about + 0.30% to + 0.44% in total travel time and + 0.32% to + 0.35% in total emissions). In this setting, direct network control (speed adjustments) is the mechanism that produces consistent improvements.

The fact that BRUE alone slightly worsens performance in the Melbourne case, whereas it improves performance in Tilburg, is mainly explained by the targeted optimization design. In Tilburg, all selected OD movements are jointly represented in a small network, so the BRUE indifference band expands the feasible path-flow region in a way that can be exploited system-wide. In Melbourne, by contrast, only 12.5% of OD demand is included in the optimization layer, while the performance indicators are evaluated on the full network. BRUE flexibility among the optimized OD pairs can therefore divert flows to near-best paths whose links are shared with the much larger unoptimized OD demand. Because the remaining demand is not simultaneously re-optimized under the same behavioral flexibility, these diversions may perturb shared links without producing a full network-wide rebalancing. This explains why BRUE alone slightly worsens the aggregate Melbourne indicators, while BRUE combined with speed control still improves performance: the speed-control layer directly modifies link operating conditions and therefore provides a stronger network-wide steering mechanism.

As in the Tilburg case, the emission magnitudes in Table 8 are conditional on the static average-speed emission kernel. They should therefore be interpreted as internally consistent scenario comparisons rather than as direct estimates from an operating-mode-aware emission model.

The reporting units differ from the Tilburg tables because the two experiments represent different temporal scopes. Tilburg indicators are reported in the annualized scaled units used in the original case study (106 h and 103 kg), whereas the Melbourne experiment represents a one-hour morning-peak application and is therefore reported in raw hours and tons.

The same conclusion holds when translating outcomes into monetary indicators using the paper’s values of time and carbon price (Table 9). Relative to UE, SC-UE-SOTT+E reduces total time cost by 10.65% and emission cost by approximately 2.5%. SC-BRUE-SOTT+E provides comparable benefits, lowering total time cost by 10.25% and emission cost by about 2.0%. Notably, these reductions are achieved even though only 12.5% of OD demand is explicitly optimized, reinforcing the interpretation that system-wide performance can be improved through a targeted optimization layer when it acts on high-impact OD pairs and a large set of controllable freeway links. At the class level, SC-BRUE-SOTT+E versus BRUE reduces car time cost by 12.34% and truck time cost by 8.65%, while also reducing car emissions by 1.91% and truck emissions by 4.34%. Within the adopted emission kernel, this class difference is driven by the heavy-vehicle emission-factor coefficients in Eq. (21), the class-specific speed limits, and the resulting link-average speeds. It should not be interpreted as evidence about stop-and-go or acceleration effects, which are not represented in the static average-speed formulation.

Moreover, Table 9 supports two observations for this large-network test: (i) speed control is the dominant lever at metropolitan scale, since both SC scenarios achieve joint reductions in total travel time and modeled emissions; and (ii) behavioural flexibility alone is not sufficient under truncated choice sets, because BRUE without SC does not improve outcomes in this instance.

The percentage changes in Table 9 are best interpreted as relative changes within the adopted static average-speed framework. Their direction and ranking are informative for the present scenario comparison, while their absolute magnitudes may differ under emission models that explicitly represent acceleration, braking, idling, or fleet heterogeneity. From a practical perspective, the Melbourne results show that, in larger networks, targeted OD-level optimization combined with link-level actuation can still yield measurable and policy-relevant network-wide benefits. This supports the practical relevance of the proposed framework.

title: Air Canada and Airbus launch joint initiative to scale domestic Canadian SAF
description:
Air Canada and Airbus are uniting their shared commitment to aviation decarbonisation.
Both companies are confident that, with a supportive public policy framework in place, this investment can serve as a catalyst for the broader Canadian SAF ecosystem.
Key focus areas include accelerating a jointly agreed Canadian SAF project toward a Final Investment Decision (FID).
“Air Canada is proud to help advance aviation’s energy transition in Canada.
“I want to thank Air Canada for this very important joint sustainability initiative.
text:
Air Canada and Airbus plan to establish a jointly funded Sustainability Co-Investment Platform, investing up to CAD 13.7 million (US$10 million) to support the development of a commercial-scale Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) industry in Canada.

The initiative will focus on advancing a Canadian SAF project towards a Final Investment Decision (FID), while supporting wider industry and government efforts to create the policy framework needed to scale domestic renewable fuel production and maintain affordable air travel.

Airbus will also support Air Canada’s Leave Less Travel Programme through a five-year agreement, while a new study highlights the economic potential of expanding Canadian SAF production, estimating up to $32 billion in GDP growth and 140,000 jobs by 2040 if SAF meets 40 percent of aviation fuel demand.

Air Canada and Airbus are uniting their shared commitment to aviation decarbonisation. To lead the way in advancing these goals, the two aviation pioneers are proud to announce their intent to establish a jointly funded Sustainability Co-Investment Platform. This agreement states a shared objective to invest up to approximately CAD 13.7 million (US$10 million), through the platform to support a commercial-scale Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) industry in Canada. Both companies are confident that, with a supportive public policy framework in place, this investment can serve as a catalyst for the broader Canadian SAF ecosystem.

Key focus areas include accelerating a jointly agreed Canadian SAF project toward a Final Investment Decision (FID). While Air Canada and Airbus intend to drive this investment, both companies look forward to continuing their constructive collaboration with government partners to establish the right structural frameworks to support SAF production to emerge at scale in Canada. Their ongoing joint advocacy alongside the Canadian Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition (C-SAF) reflects a shared commitment to working with federal and provincial governments. By aligning industry initiatives with supportive public policy mechanisms, they can successfully champion domestic SAF production and price competitiveness, with the objective to make renewable fuels available for the Canadian aerospace industry and to preserve affordability of air travel.

“Air Canada is proud to help advance aviation’s energy transition in Canada. Through this joint initiative with Airbus, we are taking meaningful steps toward supporting domestic SAF production, helping corporate customers address the emissions associated with business travel, and contributing to a lower-carbon path for the industry. With continued industry collaboration and a supportive policy environment, we are confident this momentum can accelerate” said Valerie Durand, Vice President, Airport Affairs, Corporate Real Estate and Sustainability at Air Canada.

“I want to thank Air Canada for this very important joint sustainability initiative. Decarbonising aviation will require deep industry collaboration and decades of investment in new sources of renewable energy. By launching this co-investment platform and making a long-term commitment to Air Canada’s Leave Less Travel Programme , we will help to stimulate the production of, and demand for, SAF in Canada. The country has a vast feedstock potential. When combined with a supportive policy framework, it can contribute to the sector’s decarbonisation ambitions and create significant economic growth and job creation.” said Julie Kitcher, Airbus Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications.

Climate Solution for Corporate Travel

Complementing this foundational investment, the initiative introduces a vehicle for corporate partners to stimulate domestic SAF demand through Air Canada’s Leave Less Travel Program.

Demonstrating its commitment, Airbus has signed a long-term, 5-year Leave Less Travel Program Agreement. As part of this parallel corporate travel partnership, which distributes verified SAF environmental attributes to participants, Airbus will purchase SAF environmental attributes associated with over 60,000 litres of SAF for its first allocation. Through this programme, Air Canada will track Airbus’ greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with their corporate travel and remove verified SAF environmental attributes on the company’s behalf. Although in-sector emissions reductions are not a substitute for direct emissions reductions at the source, this corporate partnership is a key tool in supporting the scaling up of SAF and will allow Airbus to lower life cycle emissions associated with their employees’ business travel.

The use of renewable fuels, such as SAF, complements Air Canada’s extensive fleet modernization strategy, featuring more fuel-efficient aircraft like the long-range narrow-body Airbus A321XLR and the Canada-built Airbus A220. Air Canada and Airbus fully support the aviation aspirational climate ambition set by IATA, ATAG and ICAO to reach ‘net-zero carbon emissions by 2050’, with SAF as a critical component to such pathway.

Multi-Billion Dollar Economic Potential

Beyond the reduction of life cycle emissions, developing a robust domestic SAF ecosystem could trigger a massive ripple effect across the Canadian economy. The strategic platform arrives alongside a new macroeconomic study by Airbus and ICF highlighting Canada’s significant potential to lead in aircraft biofuels production.

The study reveals that scaling domestic SAF to meet 40% of Canada’s aviation fuel demand by 2040 could add $32 billion to the national GDP and create 140,000 jobs across agricultural, forestry, and urban regions. By establishing a solid platform for corporate investment and support, the Air Canada and Airbus partnership serves as an immediate catalyst to support these multi-billion-dollar economic returns while advancing the development of a domestic SAF ecosystem. Consult the full report on our website.

text:
GREEN-DA, a Korean startup specializing in converting waste cooking oil into feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), has closed a pre-Series A2 round of $3.31 million (KRW 4.9 billion).

GS Ventures, D3 Jubilee Partners, Bluepoint Partners, CNT Tech, and AI Angel Club all returned as follow-on investors, while Lotte Ventures, BNK Venture Capital, and IBK(Industrial Bank of Korea) joined as new backers. The round brings GREENDA’s total funding raised to date to over $4.86 million (KRW 7.2 billion).

Founded in 2022, GREEN-DA has developed proprietary technology that recovers oil from waste cooking grease discharged by restaurants and food manufacturing plants, converting it into high-value biofuel feedstock. Rather than stopping at oil extraction, the company has built out a full SAF feedstock value chain spanning collection, pre-treatment, refining, quality control, and supply, positioning itself at the intersection of resource circulation and carbon reduction.

GREEN-DA posted $6.01 million (KRW 8.9 billion) in revenue in the first half of this year alone, representing roughly 1,000% year-over-year growth. The company now works with around 2,500 supply partners nationwide, giving it a stable feedstock sourcing network, and has obtained ISCC EU and ISCC CORSIA sustainability and carbon certifications, laying the groundwork for expansion into the European and global aviation SAF markets.

With the new capital, GREEN-DA plans to strengthen its supply capacity in both domestic and international biofuel markets and further solidify a resource circulation ecosystem where environmental and industrial goals coexist.

“This investment reflects the market’s recognition of GREEN-DA’s technological capabilities, feedstock sourcing competitiveness, and global growth potential,” said Kyu-yong Hwang, CEO of GREEN-DA. “We will use the funding to expand our feedstock collection network, upgrade our production infrastructure, accelerate technology development, and secure key talent as we grow into a global climate tech company.”

title: How to Optimize Ethanol Plant Operations in a Mature Market
description:
With about 185 ethanol plants currently operating in the U.S.—most concentrated in the Corn Belt—the industry has entered a mature phase.
The Role of Dry Grind Ethanol in Today’s Industry Dry grind processing remains the dominant production method in the U.S., valued for its relatively low capital requirements and efficient conversion of corn into fuel ethanol and animal feed.
Taken together, these challenges underscore a central reality of ethanol plant optimization: Improvements rarely come from isolated changes.
